blocks.content: Volumes follow their own lifecycle, deliberately decoupled from any single container's. Knowing exactly when a volume is created, and, critically, when it is not automatically removed, avoids both data loss and quiet disk bloat.

A volume is created (explicitly with docker volume create, or implicitly on first mount), then mounted into one or more containers over its lifetime, persisting independently the entire time, until it is explicitly removed.

blocks.alt: Created once, mounted many times, removed only when told to

blocks.content: 2. Removing a Container Does Not Remove a Named Volume
blocks.text: 2. Removing a Container Does Not Remove a Named Volume

blocks.content: This is the single most important lifecycle fact to internalize: docker rm on a container, by itself, never removes a named volume that container was using. The volume, and its data, simply keeps existing, ready to be mounted by another container later.

blocks.alt: A named volume survives its container being removed

blocks.content: As covered in the previous topic, docker rm -v does clean something up, but only anonymous volumes tied to that specific container, named volumes are deliberately excluded from this behavior, so a volume you meant to keep is never accidentally swept away.

blocks.alt: The -v flag scoped narrowly, on purpose

blocks.content: 4. Named Volumes Require an Explicit Decision to Delete
blocks.text: 4. Named Volumes Require an Explicit Decision to Delete

blocks.content: Getting rid of a named volume's data for good always requires a deliberate, separate command, docker volume rm, there is no accidental path to losing a named volume's data through ordinary container lifecycle commands.

blocks.alt: Deleting a named volume is always a deliberate, separate action

blocks.content:
docker volume rm mydata
# Permanently deletes the "mydata" volume and everything in it.
# This never happens as a side effect of removing a container.

code.content:
docker volume rm mydata
# Permanently deletes the "mydata" volume and everything in it.
# This never happens as a side effect of removing a container.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A volume's lifecycle is independent of any container's, removing a container never removes a named volume by itself.
Deleting a named volume's data always requires an explicit docker volume rm, it is never an accidental side effect.
